This output presents the strongest male classifier on the held-out test set, and it is the clearest warning result in the whole project. The prediction table shows that the model is behaving very conservatively, and the confusion matrix shows that its moderate accuracy is driven mostly by the larger negative class rather than by real success in separating `yes` and `no`. In other words, the male subgroup should be discussed as a limitation, not as a modeling success.

## Interpretation of best-model prediction outputs

This section converts the confusion matrices into short plain-language interpretations so the classification results are easier to read in the paper.

```{r}
# This chunk converts the confusion matrices into short plain-language summaries.
# It is intended to make the classification results easier to read,
# especially for readers who are less comfortable with confusion-matrix notation.
library(glue)

get_conf_counts <- function(cm_obj) {
  tab <- cm_obj$table
  list(
    TN = unname(tab["no",  "no"]),
    FN = unname(tab["no",  "yes"]),
    FP = unname(tab["yes", "no"]),
    TP = unname(tab["yes", "yes"])
  )
}

describe_conf <- function(cm_obj, label, model_name) {
  cc <- get_conf_counts(cm_obj)

  err_sentence <- if (cc$TP == 0 && cc$FP == 0) {
    "The model predicts every case as `no`, so its apparent accuracy is being driven mostly by the larger negative class rather than by meaningful class separation."
  } else if (cc$FP > cc$FN) {
    "The model makes more false positives than false negatives, which means it is somewhat more willing to predict `yes`."
  } else if (cc$FN > cc$FP) {
    "The model makes more false negatives than false positives, which means it is somewhat more conservative and misses some true `yes` cases."
  } else {
    "The model shows a fairly balanced error pattern between false positives and false negatives."
  }

  glue("
### {label}

For the **{model_name}** model, the confusion matrix contains **{cc$TN} true negatives**, **{cc$TP} true positives**, **{cc$FP} false positives**, and **{cc$FN} false negatives**. {err_sentence} This helps clarify not only how accurate the model is, but also what kind of mistakes it tends to make.
")
}

cat(describe_conf(cm_all_best, "Pooled sample interpretation", best_model_name_all))
cat(describe_conf(cm_F_best, "Female subgroup interpretation", best_model_name_F))
cat(describe_conf(cm_M_best, "Male subgroup interpretation", best_model_name_M))
```

Overall, these three confusion-matrix summaries tell a consistent classification story. The pooled model is usable, the female subgroup gives the strongest subgroup-specific classification result, and the male subgroup remains the weakest and least reliable part of the final classification framework. However, weak hard classification does not automatically mean useless probability estimation, so the next section re-evaluates the models as probability estimators rather than only as yes/no classifiers.

## Probability-based evaluation: what this section is and why it matters

The main results above evaluate the models as **hard classifiers**. In other words, each student eventually receives a final `yes` or `no` prediction after a threshold is applied to the model's predicted probability. That view is useful, but it can also hide information. A model may do only moderately well as a strict classifier while still doing a meaningful job of ranking students from lower to higher relationship chance.

My professor, Dr.Iman therefore suggested a second evaluation lens: instead of asking only whether the model classifies each student correctly, I should also ask whether the predicted probabilities themselves are informative and reasonably calibrated. This is especially relevant in the current project because some models show moderate AUC values even when their Accuracy or F1 is not especially strong, and the male subgroup provides a clear example of how an accuracy-first threshold can produce a conservative classifier that hides the underlying probability signal.

For that reason, this section shifts from **classification-focused evaluation** to **probability-focused evaluation**. I first compare the best hard-classification model with the best probability-ranking model in each group. I then report AUC, Brier score, log loss, and a simple calibration error summary. Finally, I visualize the probability results using two diagnostics : **(1) a calibration histogram of predicted probability versus actual chance** and **(2) a KDE plot of predicted probabilities for the true `no` and `yes` groups**. These plots help answer a different question from the earlier confusion matrices: not only “Did the model classify correctly?” but also “Did the model assign sensible probability values?”

## Probability-focused model selection and summary metrics

This subsection identifies the strongest **probability** model in each group by AUC rather than by Accuracy. Its role is to check whether the best model for probability estimation is the same as, or different from, the best hard-classification model.

```{r prob_eval_setup}
# This chunk re-evaluates the current models from a probability-estimation perspective.
# It identifies the best-Accuracy model and the best-AUC model in each group,
# prepares train/test probability tables, and computes probability-quality metrics.
clip_prob <- function(p) {
  pmin(pmax(as.numeric(p), 1e-6), 1 - 1e-6)
}

make_pred_tbl <- function(truth, prob) {
  tibble(
    truth = factor(truth, levels = c("no", "yes")),
    prob_yes = clip_prob(prob)
  )
}

best_acc_model <- function(results_tbl) {
  results_tbl %>%
    filter(Model %in% single_model_names) %>%
    slice_max(Accuracy, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
}

best_prob_model <- function(results_tbl) {
  results_tbl %>%
    slice_max(AUC, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
}

get_group_prob <- function(model_name, group = c("all", "F", "M"), new_df) {
  group <- match.arg(group)

  if (group == "all") {
    return(get_prob_yes(fit_lookup_all[[model_name]], new_df))
  }

  if (group == "F") {
    if (model_name %in% single_model_names) {
      return(get_prob_yes(fit_lookup_F[[model_name]], new_df))
    }
    if (model_name == "Avg Prob (RF+XGB+MLP)") {
      return(rowMeans(cbind(
        get_prob_yes(rf_fit_F, new_df),
        get_prob_yes(xgb_fit_F, new_df),
        get_prob_yes(mlp_fit_F, new_df)
      )))
    }
    if (model_name == "Stacking Ensemble") {
      return(get_prob_yes(stack_fit_F, new_df, fallback_fit = rf_fit_F))
    }
  }

  if (group == "M") {
    if (model_name %in% single_model_names) {
      return(get_prob_yes(fit_lookup_M[[model_name]], new_df))
    }
    if (model_name == "Avg Prob (kNN+RF+XGB)") {
      return(rowMeans(cbind(
        get_prob_yes(knn_fit_M, new_df),
        get_prob_yes(rf_fit_M, new_df),
        get_prob_yes(xgb_fit_M, new_df)
      )))
    }
    if (model_name == "Stacking Ensemble") {
      return(get_prob_yes(stack_fit_M, new_df, fallback_fit = knn_fit_M))
    }
  }

  stop("Unknown model name for the selected group.")
}

brier_score <- function(truth, prob) {
  y <- if_else(truth == "yes", 1, 0)
  mean((y - clip_prob(prob))^2)
}

log_loss <- function(truth, prob) {
  y <- if_else(truth == "yes", 1, 0)
  prob <- clip_prob(prob)
  -mean(y * log(prob) + (1 - y) * log(1 - prob))
}

make_calibration_df <- function(pred_df, n_bins = 6) {
  pred_df %>%
    mutate(
      truth_num = if_else(truth == "yes", 1, 0),
      bin_id = pmin(floor(prob_yes * n_bins), n_bins - 1L),
      bin_mid = (bin_id + 0.5) / n_bins
    ) %>%
    group_by(bin_id, bin_mid) %>%
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      mean_pred = mean(prob_yes),
      actual_rate = mean(truth_num),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    arrange(bin_id)
}

mean_abs_cal_error <- function(pred_df, n_bins = 6) {
  cal_df <- make_calibration_df(pred_df, n_bins = n_bins)
  weighted.mean(abs(cal_df$actual_rate - cal_df$mean_pred), cal_df$n)
}

prob_gap <- function(pred_df) {
  stats <- pred_df %>%
    group_by(truth) %>%
    summarise(mean_prob = mean(prob_yes), .groups = "drop")

  no_mean <- stats$mean_prob[stats$truth == "no"]
  yes_mean <- stats$mean_prob[stats$truth == "yes"]
  yes_mean - no_mean
}

best_all_acc  <- best_acc_model(results_all)
best_F_acc    <- best_acc_model(results_F)
best_M_acc    <- best_acc_model(results_M)

best_all_prob <- best_prob_model(results_all)
best_F_prob   <- best_prob_model(results_F)
best_M_prob   <- best_prob_model(results_M)

train_all_prob <- make_pred_tbl(
  train_data_mod$romantic,
  get_group_prob(best_all_prob$Model[[1]], "all", train_data_mod)
)

test_all_prob <- make_pred_tbl(
  test_data_mod$romantic,
  get_group_prob(best_all_prob$Model[[1]], "all", test_data_mod)
)

train_F_prob <- make_pred_tbl(
  train_F_mod$romantic,
  get_group_prob(best_F_prob$Model[[1]], "F", train_F_mod)
)

test_F_prob <- make_pred_tbl(
  test_F_mod$romantic,
  get_group_prob(best_F_prob$Model[[1]], "F", test_F_mod)
)

train_M_prob <- make_pred_tbl(
  train_M_mod$romantic,
  get_group_prob(best_M_prob$Model[[1]], "M", train_M_mod)
)

test_M_prob <- make_pred_tbl(
  test_M_mod$romantic,
  get_group_prob(best_M_prob$Model[[1]], "M", test_M_mod)
)

focus_compare <- bind_rows(
  tibble(
    Group = "Pooled",
    Best_Accuracy_Model = best_all_acc$Model[[1]],
    Best_Accuracy = best_all_acc$Accuracy[[1]],
    Best_AUC_Model = best_all_prob$Model[[1]],
    Best_AUC = best_all_prob$AUC[[1]]
  ),
  tibble(
    Group = "Female",
    Best_Accuracy_Model = best_F_acc$Model[[1]],
    Best_Accuracy = best_F_acc$Accuracy[[1]],
    Best_AUC_Model = best_F_prob$Model[[1]],
    Best_AUC = best_F_prob$AUC[[1]]
  ),
  tibble(
    Group = "Male",
    Best_Accuracy_Model = best_M_acc$Model[[1]],
    Best_Accuracy = best_M_acc$Accuracy[[1]],
    Best_AUC_Model = best_M_prob$Model[[1]],
    Best_AUC = best_M_prob$AUC[[1]]
  )
)

prob_summary <- bind_rows(
  tibble(
    Group = "Pooled",
    Model = best_all_prob$Model[[1]],
    AUC = best_all_prob$AUC[[1]],
    Brier = brier_score(test_all_prob$truth, test_all_prob$prob_yes),
    LogLoss = log_loss(test_all_prob$truth, test_all_prob$prob_yes),
    Cal_MAE = mean_abs_cal_error(test_all_prob, n_bins = 6),
    Mean_Prob_Gap = prob_gap(test_all_prob)
  ),
  tibble(
    Group = "Female",
    Model = best_F_prob$Model[[1]],
    AUC = best_F_prob$AUC[[1]],
    Brier = brier_score(test_F_prob$truth, test_F_prob$prob_yes),
    LogLoss = log_loss(test_F_prob$truth, test_F_prob$prob_yes),
    Cal_MAE = mean_abs_cal_error(test_F_prob, n_bins = 6),
    Mean_Prob_Gap = prob_gap(test_F_prob)
  ),
  tibble(
    Group = "Male",
    Model = best_M_prob$Model[[1]],
    AUC = best_M_prob$AUC[[1]],
    Brier = brier_score(test_M_prob$truth, test_M_prob$prob_yes),
    LogLoss = log_loss(test_M_prob$truth, test_M_prob$prob_yes),
    Cal_MAE = mean_abs_cal_error(test_M_prob, n_bins = 6),
    Mean_Prob_Gap = prob_gap(test_M_prob)
  )
)

focus_compare
prob_summary
```

**Probability-focused model-selection table.** This first table compares the best hard-classification model in each group with the best probability-ranking model in each group. If these two models differ, that means the model that gives the highest Accuracy is not the same as the model that gives the best probability information.

**Probability-metrics table.** This second table reports four probability-oriented summaries for the best-AUC model in each group. AUC tells me how well the model ranks students from lower to higher relationship chance, Brier score and log loss tell me how close the predicted probabilities are to the actual outcomes, and `Cal_MAE` gives a simple binned calibration-error summary. Lower Brier, log loss, and calibration error are better, while higher AUC is better.

```{r prob_eval_summary_text, results='asis'}
# This chunk converts the probability-focused tables into a short plain-language summary.
# It is meant to directly address whether Dr.Iman's suggestion is supported.
match_n <- sum(focus_compare$Best_Accuracy_Model == focus_compare$Best_AUC_Model)

strongest_prob <- prob_summary %>% slice_max(AUC, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
weakest_prob   <- prob_summary %>% slice_min(AUC, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

cat(glue::glue(
"**Probability-summary interpretation.** These tables partially support my professor Dr. Iman's point. The best hard-classification model and the best probability-ranking model match in only **{match_n} of the 3 groups**, which means Accuracy and probability quality are not telling exactly the same story. The clearest support appears in the **{strongest_prob$Group[[1]]}** group, where **{strongest_prob$Model[[1]]}** gives the strongest probability ranking with an AUC of **{round(strongest_prob$AUC[[1]], 3)}**. The weakest probability performance still appears in the **{weakest_prob$Group[[1]]}** group, with an AUC of **{round(weakest_prob$AUC[[1]], 3)}**. Overall, the pooled and female results are the clearest cases where the models look more informative in probability space than they do under hard classification alone.\n\n"
))
```

## Calibration histogram: predicted probability vs actual chance

A calibration histogram checks whether the **probability values themselves** are trustworthy. If a model places students into a bin around 30%, then roughly 30% of those students should actually be in a relationship. In the plots below, the bars show the actual relationship rate inside each probability bin, while the black points show the average predicted probability in that bin. When the bars and points are close, the model is better calibrated.

```{r prob_plot_helpers}
# This chunk defines helper functions for the probability plots and for the short
# plain-language explanations placed directly after each figure.
plot_calibration_hist <- function(pred_df, title_text, n_bins = 6) {
  cal_df <- make_calibration_df(pred_df, n_bins = n_bins)

  ggplot(cal_df, aes(x = bin_mid)) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_col(aes(y = actual_rate), width = 0.9 / n_bins, alpha = 0.60) +
    geom_point(aes(y = mean_pred, size = n), color = "black") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(
      title = title_text,
      x = "Predicted probability bin",
      y = "Actual chance (bar) and average predicted probability (point)",
      size = "N"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

plot_prob_kde <- function(pred_df, title_text) {
  ggplot(pred_df, aes(x = prob_yes, fill = truth, color = truth)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.20, linewidth = 1.1, adjust = 1.1) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(
      title = title_text,
      x = "Predicted probability of being in a relationship",
      y = "Density",
      fill = "Actual class",
      color = "Actual class"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

describe_calibration_plot <- function(pred_df, group_label, model_name) {
  cal_df <- make_calibration_df(pred_df, n_bins = 6)
  mae <- weighted.mean(abs(cal_df$actual_rate - cal_df$mean_pred), cal_df$n)
  trend_cor <- suppressWarnings(cor(cal_df$mean_pred, cal_df$actual_rate, use = "complete.obs"))

  quality_text <- case_when(
    is.na(mae) ~ "difficult to judge because the bins are sparse",
    mae < 0.05 ~ "fairly well calibrated",
    mae < 0.10 ~ "reasonably calibrated but still somewhat noisy",
    mae < 0.15 ~ "only loosely calibrated",
    TRUE ~ "quite noisy and not especially well calibrated"
  )

  trend_text <- if (!is.na(trend_cor) && trend_cor > 0.60) {
    "The observed relationship rate generally rises as the predicted probability bins rise"
  } else if (!is.na(trend_cor) && trend_cor > 0.30) {
    "The observed relationship rate rises somewhat with the predicted bins, although the pattern is not perfectly smooth"
  } else {
    "The observed relationship rate does not rise smoothly with the predicted bins"
  }

  glue::glue(
"**{group_label} calibration histogram.** For this plot, each bar shows the actual relationship rate within one predicted-probability bin, while the black point shows the average predicted probability in that same bin. {trend_text}. The average absolute gap between the predicted and observed bin-level values is about **{scales::percent(mae, accuracy = 1)}**, so the **{model_name}** probabilities are {quality_text} in the {tolower(group_label)}.\n\n"
  )
}

describe_kde_plot <- function(pred_df, group_label, model_name, auc_value) {
  stats <- pred_df %>%
    group_by(truth) %>%
    summarise(mean_prob = mean(prob_yes), .groups = "drop")

  no_mean  <- stats$mean_prob[stats$truth == "no"]
  yes_mean <- stats$mean_prob[stats$truth == "yes"]
  gap <- yes_mean - no_mean

  shift_text <- case_when(
    is.na(gap) ~ "cannot be judged clearly",
    gap >= 0.15 ~ "a clear rightward shift",
    gap >= 0.08 ~ "a noticeable rightward shift",
    gap >= 0.03 ~ "a small but visible rightward shift",
    TRUE ~ "very little rightward shift"
  )

  auc_text <- case_when(
    auc_value >= 0.75 ~ "strong ranking ability",
    auc_value >= 0.65 ~ "moderate ranking ability",
    auc_value >= 0.55 ~ "limited but non-zero ranking ability",
    TRUE ~ "very weak ranking ability"
  )

  glue::glue(
"**{group_label} KDE plot.** For this plot, the two density curves show how the predicted probabilities are distributed for students who are actually in the `no` group and the `yes` group. In the {tolower(group_label)}, the true-`yes` cases receive an average predicted probability of **{scales::percent(yes_mean, accuracy = 1)}**, compared with **{scales::percent(no_mean, accuracy = 1)}** for the true-`no` cases, which is {shift_text}. Together with an AUC of **{round(auc_value, 3)}**, this suggests {auc_text} for the **{model_name}** probability estimates.\n\n"
  )
}
```

## KDE plot of predicted probabilities

A KDE plot looks at a different issue from calibration. Instead of asking whether the probabilities are on the correct scale, it asks whether the model gives **higher probabilities to the students who are actually in the `yes` group**. The more the `yes` curve shifts to the right of the `no` curve, the more useful the model is as a probability-ranking tool, even if the two curves still overlap.

### Pooled sample KDE plot

```{r pooled_kde_plot}
# This chunk shows the probability-density separation for the pooled best-AUC model.
# It compares the predicted probabilities for the true no and true yes groups.
plot_prob_kde(
  test_all_prob,
  paste0("KDE of predicted probabilities: pooled sample (", best_all_prob$Model[[1]], ")")
)
```

```{r pooled_kde_text, results='asis'}
cat(describe_kde_plot(test_all_prob, "Pooled sample", best_all_prob$Model[[1]], best_all_prob$AUC[[1]]))
```

## Simple improvement: post-hoc probability calibration

If the plots above show that the models rank students reasonably well but the absolute probability scale is still somewhat off, a simple improvement is to **recalibrate the probabilities after model fitting** instead of retraining every model from scratch. The idea is straightforward: I keep the original model predictions, then fit a small logistic calibration model on the training-set probabilities and apply that correction to the test set. This does not try to change the ordering of students very much; instead, it tries to make the reported probabilities themselves more realistic.

```{r posthoc_calibration}
# This chunk applies a simple logistic recalibration step to the best-AUC model in each group.
# It compares the raw probabilities with the recalibrated probabilities using Brier score and log loss.
fit_logistic_calibrator <- function(pred_df) {
  cal_df <- pred_df %>%
    mutate(
      y = if_else(truth == "yes", 1, 0),
      lp = qlogis(clip_prob(prob_yes))
    )

  if (dplyr::n_distinct(cal_df$lp) < 2) {
    return(NULL)
  }

  glm(y ~ lp, data = cal_df, family = binomial())
}

apply_logistic_calibrator <- function(prob, cal_fit) {
  prob <- clip_prob(prob)

  if (is.null(cal_fit)) {
    return(prob)
  }

  as.numeric(
    plogis(
      predict(
        cal_fit,
        newdata = tibble(lp = qlogis(prob)),
        type = "link"
      )
    )
  )
}

cal_fit_all <- fit_logistic_calibrator(train_all_prob)
cal_fit_F   <- fit_logistic_calibrator(train_F_prob)
cal_fit_M   <- fit_logistic_calibrator(train_M_prob)

test_all_prob_cal <- test_all_prob %>%
  mutate(prob_cal = apply_logistic_calibrator(prob_yes, cal_fit_all))

test_F_prob_cal <- test_F_prob %>%
  mutate(prob_cal = apply_logistic_calibrator(prob_yes, cal_fit_F))

test_M_prob_cal <- test_M_prob %>%
  mutate(prob_cal = apply_logistic_calibrator(prob_yes, cal_fit_M))

calibration_compare <- bind_rows(
  tibble(
    Group = "Pooled",
    Model = best_all_prob$Model[[1]],
    Raw_Brier = brier_score(test_all_prob_cal$truth, test_all_prob_cal$prob_yes),
    Calibrated_Brier = brier_score(test_all_prob_cal$truth, test_all_prob_cal$prob_cal),
    Raw_LogLoss = log_loss(test_all_prob_cal$truth, test_all_prob_cal$prob_yes),
    Calibrated_LogLoss = log_loss(test_all_prob_cal$truth, test_all_prob_cal$prob_cal)
  ),
  tibble(
    Group = "Female",
    Model = best_F_prob$Model[[1]],
    Raw_Brier = brier_score(test_F_prob_cal$truth, test_F_prob_cal$prob_yes),
    Calibrated_Brier = brier_score(test_F_prob_cal$truth, test_F_prob_cal$prob_cal),
    Raw_LogLoss = log_loss(test_F_prob_cal$truth, test_F_prob_cal$prob_yes),
    Calibrated_LogLoss = log_loss(test_F_prob_cal$truth, test_F_prob_cal$prob_cal)
  ),
  tibble(
    Group = "Male",
    Model = best_M_prob$Model[[1]],
    Raw_Brier = brier_score(test_M_prob_cal$truth, test_M_prob_cal$prob_yes),
    Calibrated_Brier = brier_score(test_M_prob_cal$truth, test_M_prob_cal$prob_cal),
    Raw_LogLoss = log_loss(test_M_prob_cal$truth, test_M_prob_cal$prob_yes),
    Calibrated_LogLoss = log_loss(test_M_prob_cal$truth, test_M_prob_cal$prob_cal)
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    Brier_Improvement = Raw_Brier - Calibrated_Brier,
    LogLoss_Improvement = Raw_LogLoss - Calibrated_LogLoss
  )

calibration_compare
```

**Post-hoc calibration table.** This table compares the original probability scores with a simple logistic recalibration fitted on the training-set probabilities. Positive improvement values mean the recalibrated probabilities are better by that metric. This is a lightweight improvement because it does not require rerunning the heavy model-tuning pipeline.

```{r posthoc_calibration_text, results='asis'}
# This chunk translates the calibration-comparison table into a short interpretation.
# It explains whether the simple recalibration step helps and why it matters.
helpful_groups <- calibration_compare %>%
  filter(Brier_Improvement > 0 | LogLoss_Improvement > 0) %>%
  pull(Group)

helpful_text <- if (length(helpful_groups) == 0) {
  "In this render, the recalibration gains are small or mixed across groups, so the main value of the section is diagnostic rather than corrective."
} else {
  paste0(
    "In this render, the recalibration step helps most clearly in: **",
    paste(helpful_groups, collapse = ", "),
    "**."
  )
}

cat(glue::glue(
"**Post-hoc calibration interpretation.** This comparison shows whether a simple probability recalibration can improve the model outputs without retraining the full models. {helpful_text} Because this correction is monotonic, it mainly adjusts the probability scale rather than the ranking of students, so it is best understood as a probability-quality improvement rather than a new classification model.\n\n"
))
```

## Final probability-based takeaway

Taken together, these probability diagnostics provide a more nuanced reading of the project: the current models, especially in the pooled sample and the female subgroup, are more informative as **probability estimators** than the hard-classification results alone might suggest. At the same time, the male subgroup still remains the most difficult part of the project even under a probability-focused lens, which is consistent with its smaller sample, stronger instability across versions, and the stricter student-level data construction used in Final version. The most practical improvement added here is the post-hoc calibration step, and the clearest future probability-first upgrade would be to tune and compare models directly by probability metrics such as log loss or Brier score instead of selecting everything from an accuracy-first perspective.
